## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhaggajātaka* (also cited as the *Gagga-jātaka*, Ja 155) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010]. According to its opening frame, the Buddha recounted the story while residing at a monastery built by King Pasenadi in front of Jetavana, prompted by an incident involving a sneeze [SuttaCentral]. Naomi Appleton observes that this story of the present connects to a monastic disciplinary discussion also preserved in the Cullavagga, where a sermon is disrupted after a sneeze provokes listeners to shout "long life to you!" [Appleton 2010].

In the story of the past, a brahmin named Gagga and his son—the Bodhisatta—take shelter in a dwelling haunted by a *yakkha* who is entitled to devour anyone who fails to wish "long life" after a sneeze [Appleton 2010]. When the demon makes Gagga sneeze, the quick-witted Bodhisatta immediately recites the blessing ("Gagga, live an hundred years"), prompting his father to respond in kind, thereby safeguarding both of them and subsequently reforming the demon [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010]. Appleton highlights the tale as an example of a mundane, quick-witted folktale incorporated into the canon and "Buddhicised" through its Vinaya-related frame story [Appleton 2010].

SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages and lists no external canonical parallels [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse across four passages (totalling 456 characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), with no cross-language matches registered [DharmaNexus].
